title: The garden and the one tree
word: The garden and the one tree
hook: Adam and his wife live in the garden with everything, told only to leave one tree (2:35)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Iblis, the one who would not bow, fire looking down on mud. Your line was pride was the first mistake. Did you catch an I'm better than? Day twenty-five.

Picture a friend handing you the keys to their house for a month. The fridge is full. Use the car, the pool, the good coffee, the books, everything. Honestly, anything. Just one thing: don't open that cupboard in the hall. That's all. Now be honest. Where does your mind go, first thing, on the first night? Not to the pool. To the cupboard. It's almost funny how human that is. And it's where Adam's story goes next. After the angels and the names and the one who wouldn't bow, Adam gets a home. A garden with everything in it. And one rule.
screen: `THE KEYS TO A FRIEND'S HOUSE.` → `EVERYTHING, EXCEPT ONE CUPBOARD.` → `A GARDEN, AND ONE RULE.`

segments.voice: Surah two, verse thirty-five. God says: Adam, live in the garden, you and your wife, and in Pickthall's words, “eat ye freely (of the fruits) thereof where ye will; but come not nigh this tree lest ye become wrongdoers.” Freely, where you will. The permission is huge, and it comes first. Another surah describes the garden's promise: you won't go hungry there or be naked, you won't be thirsty or burned by the sun. Everything. And then, the one tree. Not even don't eat, exactly: don't come near it. Keep your distance. Here's what the Qur'an doesn't say. It doesn't name Adam's wife; the name Hawwa, Eve, comes from the hadith and later tradition. It doesn't name the tree, or the fruit. There's no apple in the Qur'an; the apple comes from later paintings. Commentators guessed at wheat, or grapes, or figs, and many said the point is that we aren't told. Scholars even differ about the garden itself. Many say it was the paradise of the hereafter. Others say it was a garden somewhere on earth. The Qur'an leaves these open, and keeps its eye on one thing: a whole world of yes, and a single no. Why a no at all? One common answer from the scholars: a steward, a khalifah, has to be someone who can be trusted with a limit. A life with no limits at all isn't a trust. It's just a playground. The one tree is what turns the garden into a test of love, and of trust.
screen: `EAT FREELY, WHERE YOU WILL.` · `BUT COME NOT NIGH THIS TREE.` · `NO NAME, NO APPLE.` · `A LIMIT MAKES IT A TRUST.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING, MINUS ONE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Make a quiet list, in your head, of what you already have enough of. Start small. Enough light to see by. Enough air in this breath. A bed. Something to eat later. Someone who'd answer if you called. Keep going, slowly, and let the list get long. Notice how big the garden already is. Then, if it comes, notice the one thing your mind keeps drifting back to, the thing you don't have. Just see it, and come back to the list. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for the garden. The bell holds the time.
The garden and the one tree. A world of freely, where you will, and a single place not to go near.
screen: `THE GARDEN AND THE ONE TREE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: everything, minus one. Today, when you catch yourself fixed on the one thing you can't have, look up and count three things you can. Day twenty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims read the garden story in surahs two, seven and twenty; teachers often draw from it that the permitted, halal, is wide and the forbidden is narrow.

original.note: Arabic: "this tree," the words of 2:35. shajarah is the ordinary word for a tree.

trapdoor: what you thought: Adam and Eve ate an apple.
what it means: the garden and the one tree — everything given freely, and one limit: don't come near this tree.

what a scholar hears: the Qur'an names neither the wife, the tree nor the fruit; commentators guessed wheat, grapes or figs; and scholars differ whether the garden was the paradise of the hereafter or a garden on earth.

sources.ref: Qur'an 20:117–119 (no hunger, nakedness, thirst or sun in the garden)
al-Tabari, Tafsir on 2:35 (the tree: wheat, vine, fig and others)

notes: Pickthall 2:35 quoted from memory ('And We said: O Adam! Dwell thou and thy wife in the Garden, and eat ye freely (of the fruits) thereof where ye will; but come not nigh this tree lest ye become wrongdoers.'). Confirm.
Hawwa: named in hadith and tafsir, not in the Qur'an. Confirm.
Candidates for the tree (wheat/ear of corn, vine, fig, and others) are from al-Tabari's collection of views; al-Tabari concludes God did not specify it. Confirm.

The garden: majority view that it was Jannat al-Khuld (the paradise of the hereafter); a minority (e.g. some Mu'tazilites and others) held it was an earthly garden. Confirm the phrasing 'many say / others say'.
'The apple comes from later paintings': a general statement (the Bible doesn't name the fruit either; the apple is a later Western convention). Keeps no comparison. Confirm.
'A limit makes it a trust' is offered as 'one common answer from the scholars'; a Keeper may want a named source or softer wording.
